title: Trade Law as a Hydrological Strategy: Multi-Criteria Assessment of Instruments Governing Virtual Water Exports from Pakistan’s Indus Basin
content: Climate change is reshaping the hydrology of the Indus River Basin, the world’s most relied-upon mountain water tower, while Pakistan exports large volumes of water embedded in rice, sugar and cotton. This virtual water outflow is governed largely by trade law, yet trade-law instruments are rarely assessed as hydrological strategies. This study develops a legal–hydrological multicriteria framework that evaluates eight such instruments against six criteria: blue-water saving, groundwater and water-quality co-benefits, climate-adaptive flexibility, legal risk under World Trade Organization (WTO) and free-trade-agreement rules, socio-economic burden and institutional feasibility. Scores combine basin hydro-climatic evidence with a doctrinal analysis of WTO agreements, jurisprudence and Pakistani water legislation. Instruments were ranked with TOPSIS under six weighting scenarios, including entropy and climate-stress weights, and tested through 10,000 joint perturbations of weights and scores. Capped support for water-saving irrigation ranked first in five of six scenarios (first-rank acceptability 49.6%), followed by realignment of administered crop prices and crop-differentiated water pricing; only four instruments were Pareto-efficient. An econometric validation of the simulation (OLS, logit, multinomial and ordered-logit metamodels, variance decomposition and cross-method triangulation) shows that the lead changes only if the weight on blue-water saving exceeds about 25% or on institutional feasibility about 32%. Drought-triggered export restrictions and trade–water issue linkage performed worst. For Pakistan’s water resources management in a changing climate, the most effective trade-law strategy is therefore a WTO-compatible package of demand-side domestic instruments, not border restrictions on water-intensive exports.
